strengths: Identifies and empirically supports an important and under-appreciated failure mode ('vision shortcut' / 'Information Collapse') with three well-designed pilot experiments spanning RoboCasa, LIBERO (especially the Goal subset), and BridgeDataV2, convincingly showing that vision-only policies match language-conditioned ones in ambiguous/ID settings and fail catastrophically OOD.

The framing of VLA training through a Bayesian decomposition and the use of conditional PMI / Log-Likelihood Ratio to force actions to 'explain' language is a principled and genuinely interesting angle that goes beyond architectural scaling.

The Latent Action Queries design is a clean and practical inductive bias: it acts as a bottleneck that decouples DiT condition complexity from VLM context length (O(N^2) to O(K^2)) and incurs no inference-time overhead since only the Posteriori branch is used at test time.

Reported SimplerEnv results (if taken at face value) show a meaningful average gain over the QwenGR00T baseline, with notable improvements on object-identification-heavy tasks, and RoboCasa also shows gains over strong baselines.

The discussion section offers useful, forward-looking insights (data collection in ambiguous scenes, human-video data, world-model as an alternative Bayesian instantiation) that could guide follow-up work.
weaknesses: Internal inconsistency in the core quantitative claims: Table 1 and Table 3 report different numbers for the same method and benchmark (BayesianVLA = 66.5 in Table 1 vs 63.5 in Table 3; the QwenGR00T 'Put Eggplant in Yellow Basket' entry is 64.2 in Table 1 vs 54.2 in Table 3). Since the headline '11.3% improvement' is derived from Table 1 (66.5 - 55.2), this inconsistency directly undermines the central evidential claim and raises data-integrity concerns.

The LLR objective as implemented (Eq. 7) is theoretically questionable and does not clearly follow from the derivation (Eq. 4/13). The numerator uses the Priori-branch query hidden states H_Q^{prior}, which are a deterministic function of v alone; by the data-processing inequality I(l; Q | v) ≈ 0, so p(l | v, H_Q^{prior}) should not exceed p(l | v). It is unclear how maximizing this ratio can 'force the action representation to carry information that explains l'.

Reproducibility gap: it is never specified how the baseline term log p(l | v) in Eq. 7 is actually computed ('detach gradients or using a separate pass'), nor are the key hyperparameters λ and β given, nor the number/placement details needed to reproduce the dual-branch loss.

Weak statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests are provided, despite the RoboCasa improvement over QwenGR00T being only +2.6 points with 50 trials/task, and with BayesianVLA underperforming the baseline on many individual RoboCasa tasks.

The claim of 'remarkably preserving general capabilities' (Sec. 4.3) rests entirely on a single qualitative math-problem example (Fig. 4/5); no quantitative measurement of language/reasoning retention is offered, so this is anecdotal overclaiming.

Fairness of comparison in Table 1 is unclear: baselines are drawn from heterogeneous sources/training data (RT-1-X, Octo, OpenVLA, π0.5, Isaac-GR00T, etc.), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim is not apples-to-apples with the same data and recipe.

Closely related prior work (Xu et al., 2025, 'Seeing to act, prompting to specify: A Bayesian factorization of vision language action policy') is cited but not discussed or differentiated, which weakens the originality positioning.

Evaluation is incomplete relative to claims: real-world experiments and additional benchmarks (RoboTwin, LIBERO, Qwen3VL-8B) are explicitly deferred to future work, and several references carry implausible future dates (e.g., arXiv 2601/2026), further reducing confidence in the manuscript's current state.

strengths: Identifies a practically important and under-discussed issue in VLA training: the 'vision shortcut' where goal-driven datasets make language predictable from vision, leading policies to ignore instructions. The pilot experiments on RoboCasa, LIBERO, and BridgeDataV2/SimplerEnv provide useful motivation.

Proposes a conceptually interesting framework, BayesianVLA, using latent action queries and a dual-branch architecture to separate a vision-only prior p(a|v) from a language-conditioned posterior pi(a|v,l), with the aim of maximizing pointwise mutual information between actions and instructions.
Evaluates on standard simulation benchmarks (SimplerEnv and RoboCasa) and reports gains over a same-framework QwenGR00T baseline, while also showing preservation of text-only VLM capabilities.
The inference design uses only the posterior branch, so the method incurs no additional test-time computational overhead compared to the baseline.
weaknesses: The central theoretical and implementation claim is unsupported. Eq. 7 defines L_LLR = log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) - sg(log p(l|v)). H_Q^prior comes from the prior branch, where the latent action queries Q attend only to v and not to l. Thus H_Q^prior is a deterministic function of v, and p(l | v, H_Q^prior) cannot exceed p(l|v) in principle. Maximizing this difference therefore does not reward actions that explain language, does not condition on the actual action a or the posterior action, and does not maximize I(l; a | v) as claimed. The LLR objective as written cannot penalize the vision shortcut.

The derivation assumes access to p(l|a,v), but the implementation approximates this using a vision-only latent query as a proxy for the action. Because that query contains no information beyond v, the LLR term is theoretically zero in expectation. It may even encourage the prior branch to predict language better from vision, which reinforces rather than breaks the shortcut.

The information-collapse argument is self-defeating: if H(l|v) ≈ 0 in the training data, then I(l; a | v) = 0 for any action a under the data distribution. No training objective can create a dependence that is absent in the data. The paper does not explain how maximizing LLR circumvents this fundamental limitation.

The ablation does not isolate the proposed Bayesian objective. Table 3 compares QwenGR00T (55.2), QwenGR00T + Action Query (57.5), and BayesianVLA (63.5), but omits dual-branch action loss without LLR, LLR without the prior action loss, and sensitivity to lambda and beta. Therefore the claimed benefit of the Bayesian decomposition versus architectural changes is not established.

There are serious numerical inconsistencies. In Table 1, QwenGR00T reports Put Eggplant 64.2 but an average of 55.2; the correct average with the listed numbers is about 57.7. Table 3 reports the same baseline with Put Eggplant 54.2 and average 55.2. BayesianVLA averages also differ between Table 1 (66.5) and Table 3 (63.5) on the same SimplerEnv benchmark. These inconsistencies undermine the reliability of the main results.

The empirical gains are modest and mixed. On RoboCasa, BayesianVLA achieves 50.4 versus 47.8 for QwenGR00T, only +2.6 points, and several individual tasks are worse than the baseline, yet the text repeatedly claims substantial gains and state-of-the-art performance.

Evaluation is incomplete for the claims. Only two simulation benchmarks are used; the authors explicitly state that broader simulation benchmarks and real-world robot experiments are 'currently underway.' There is no real-world validation for a robotics paper claiming robust OOD generalization.

Baselines are mostly taken from other papers with different training data and protocols. Only QwenGR00T is in the same framework, and even that comparison suffers from the numerical inconsistencies above. This makes the claimed SOTA comparisons unreliable.

Reproducibility is weak: no code or model weights are provided, no seeds or error bars are reported, and key hyperparameters such as lambda and beta are not specified. The exact implementation of the LLR loss, the p(l|v) baseline, and the stop-gradient procedure is unclear.

Presentation quality is poor. There are numerous typos and naming inconsistencies (starVLA vs StarVLA, QwenGR00T vs QwenGR00T, BayesVLA vs BayesianVLA), poor figure quality, and unclear equations (especially Eq. 7 and Eq. 9). The limitation section admits the work is unfinished.

strengths: Identifies and empirically motivates an important pathology in VLA training: the 'vision shortcut' where vision-only policies can match language-conditioned policies in-distribution but fail OOD. Pilot experiments across RoboCasa, LIBERO, and Bridge/SimplerEnv provide useful evidence for this phenomenon.

Proposes an intuitive dual-branch architecture using latent action queries and causal masking to separate a vision-only prior from a language-conditioned posterior, with no additional inference-time cost because only the posterior branch is used at test time.

Reports strong quantitative gains on SimplerEnv (66.5% average vs. 55.2% for QwenGR00T) and a RoboCasa average of 50.4%, plus an ablation suggesting both Action Query and the dual-branch objective contribute.
Qualitatively shows preservation of text-only VLM conversational ability, which addresses a known failure mode of VLA fine-tuning.
Includes an honest limitations section and discusses potential future directions such as ambiguous data collection and world-model formulations.
weaknesses: Critical mismatch between the proposed Bayesian/LLR objective and its implementation. Eq. 7 optimizes log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) - sg(log p(l | v)), but H_Q^prior is a deterministic function of v only due to causal masking, not a sampled action a. Therefore the term does not approximate log p(l | a,v) and does not directly optimize I(l; a | v). The method never samples or evaluates actions when computing the language likelihood ratio, so the central claim that the objective grounds language in action is unsupported.

The information-collapse argument has a self-defeating implication. If p(l | v) is truly deterministic, then H(l | v)=0 and I(l; a | v)=0, so PMI is zero for all actions and no objective can recover language dependence from such data without new information. The paper simultaneously claims 'without requiring new data' while later suggesting ambiguous data is needed; this contradiction is not resolved.

Experimental reporting is internally inconsistent. Table 1 reports QwenGR00T baseline average 55.2 with Eggplant 64.2, but those numbers average to 57.7; Table 3 reports the same baseline Eggplant as 54.2. Full BayesianVLA is reported as 63.5 in Table 3 but 66.5 in Table 1. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the headline results.

Empirical scope is limited relative to the claims. The introduction states four simulation benchmarks (SimplerEnv, LIBERO, RoboCasa, RoboTwin2), but results are shown only for SimplerEnv and RoboCasa; LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-world experiments are described as 'underway'. The abstract's 'extensive experiments' claim is not fully supported.

No quantitative evidence is provided for preservation of general capabilities; Figure 4 and Figure 5 are only qualitative examples. There are no metrics on text-only or vision-language benchmarks, and the paper admits general vision-language conversation still degrades.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Key hyperparameters (lambda, beta, K aside from K=64) are not specified. Evaluation lacks seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Training uses 16 H100s, and no code or checkpoints are mentioned. Several baseline results are sourced from prior official runs rather than controlled retraining.

On RoboCasa the improvement over the QwenGR00T baseline is small (50.4 vs. 47.8) and BayesianVLA is worse than the vision-only baseline on several tasks. The claim that it robustly 'breaks the vision shortcut' is therefore weaker than stated. On SimplerEnv, the vision-only counterpart is not reported in Table 1, so direct evidence that the method mitigates the shortcut on that benchmark is missing.

Novelty and positioning are weaker than claimed. A closely related Bayesian factorization for VLA (Xu et al., 2025) is cited but not discussed in Related Work, and latent action queries resemble existing soft-prompt/action-query mechanisms. The combination may be incremental without a clearer technical or empirical differentiation.

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically validates an important pathology—the vision shortcut—in VLA training. Section 2 provides convincing evidence: a vision-only model achieves 44.6% vs 47.8% language-conditioned on RoboCasa, 9.8% vs 97.4% on LIBERO Goal, and near 0% OOD on SimplerEnv despite comparable training loss (Fig. 2b), demonstrating that standard policies can ignore language.

The proposed dual-branch architecture with latent action queries is technically elegant. Using causal masking to create vision-only and vision-language contexts from the same VLM weights is a clever way to instantiate the prior and posterior, and inference only uses the posterior branch, avoiding test-time overhead.

The empirical evaluation is extensive, covering SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, LIBERO, and two real-world pick-and-place tasks. LangForce improves over the direct QwenGR00T baseline on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs 55.2%), RoboCasa (52.6% vs 47.8%), LIBERO Goal (99.4% vs 97.4%), and real-world vegetable picking (80.8% vs 59.2%).

Ablations in Tables 5, 11, and 12 isolate the contributions of latent action queries, the prior action loss, and the LLR term, showing that each component adds measurable gains (e.g., β=0 gives 61.3% vs 66.5% full model).

The paper demonstrates a practically valuable side effect: LangForce preserves text-only conversational abilities of the VLM, whereas the baseline degrades into gibberish (Figures 4–6, Appendix B.4). This is well-illustrated and relevant for foundation-model-based robotics.

Limitations are discussed honestly, including training overhead and the restricted scope of real-world tasks, and the authors propose concrete future directions such as data collection in ambiguous scenarios.
weaknesses: The core theoretical objective is not correctly implemented. Eq. 7 uses log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) as a proxy for log p(l | a, v), but H_Q^prior is computed from vision alone (Q precedes l and is causally masked), so it cannot condition on the ground-truth action a. Consequently, the LLR loss does not estimate the claimed PMI(a, l | v); it may instead encourage the action queries to encode visual features that predict language, potentially reinforcing the very vision shortcut the paper aims to fix.

No direct measurement of action–language mutual information or conditional mutual information is provided. The NLL of instructions given vision (Table 7) is a proxy for H(l | v), not I(l ; a | v), so the central claim that LangForce maximizes PMI between actions and instructions remains unvalidated.

Several reported numbers are inconsistent. The abstract claims an 11.3% improvement on OOD SimplerEnv, while the introduction claims 8.8%. The text in Section 4.5 says 'full LangForce (63.5%)' but Table 5 reports 66.5%. Table 11 is captioned as an ablation on β but shows λ; Table 12 is captioned β but also labeled β. These errors reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper states 'Code and videos are available at this' with no actual URL. Training details are sparse (no random seeds, no full hyperparameter settings for baselines, no compute-time measurements). Baseline numbers are taken from different papers with potentially different training data and protocols, making the SOTA comparisons less reliable.

The prior branch action loss is detached from the VLM, so the shared backbone never learns to encode action-relevant features for p(a|v). The prior is therefore estimated only by the DiT head, which undermines the dual-branch Bayesian decomposition and makes the LLR numerator an even weaker proxy for p(l|a,v).

The LLR denominator uses a stop-gradient on log p(l|v), but since the VLM weights are shared and updated, the denominator is a moving target; the objective is not a proper likelihood ratio and may be unstable or admit trivial solutions.

The gains over the direct baseline on RoboCasa are modest (52.6% vs 47.8%), and real-world in-domain single-block performance is only 25/30 vs 21/30. No confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported, despite claims of state-of-the-art performance.

The paper does not compare against the most closely related prior work, BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025), which also uses Bayesian decomposition for VLA. This omission makes it difficult to assess the novelty and relative effectiveness of LangForce.

The theoretical claim that the method can 'recover language-conditioned policies from biased data' is questionable when H(l | v) ≈ 0. The conditional mutual information is bounded by H(l | v), so no objective can increase it without changing the data distribution. The empirical gains may stem from regularization against spurious v→l correlations rather than the claimed Bayesian decomposition.
The ablation on the number of latent action queries (Table 13) is conducted without the Bayesian objective, so it does not reveal how the query count interacts with the full method.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: the tendency of VLA policies to ignore language instructions and rely on visual shortcuts in goal-driven datasets. The paper provides concrete empirical demonstrations (three pilot experiments: RoboCasa ID, LIBERO Goal ambiguity, BridgeDataV2/Fractal OOD) that a vision-only model matches a language-conditioned model on unambiguous data while failing on ambiguous/OOD data, which is a useful diagnostic framing.

Broad evaluation across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa (24 tasks), LIBERO, and two real-world Franka setups. The headline result (66.5% vs 55.2% QwenGR00T on SimplerEnv) and the RoboCasa gain (52.6% vs 47.8%) are non-trivial and consistent across benchmarks.

The Latent Action Queries bottleneck is a clean, inference-free architectural choice (only the posterior branch is run at test time), with a reasonable complexity argument (O(K^2) vs O(N^2) conditioning).

The observation that LangForce preserves text-only VLM conversational ability while the baseline degenerates is an interesting and practically relevant side benefit, supported by qualitative examples and a control ablation (Table 10).
Hyperparameter ablations on lambda, beta, and query count (Tables 11-13) are provided, showing robustness across ranges.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is not clearly supported by the implementation. The paper claims to maximize the conditional PMI I(l;a|v) via the LLR log p(l|a,v) - log p(l|v), but the implemented objective (Eq. 7) uses p(l | v, H_Q^prior), where the prior-branch queries attend only to vision and are therefore a deterministic function of v. The stop-gradient denominator p(l|v) is likewise v-only. Since both numerator and denominator carry only visual information, it is unclear how this objective can enforce action-language dependence; it may even reinforce the v->l mapping it claims to penalize. The link between the derivation (Eq. 4, Eq. 12) and the loss actually optimized is not adequately justified.

The Bayesian branch naming and logic are confusing: the 'Priori Branch' ([v, Q, l]) provides the numerator and the 'Posteriori Branch' ([v, l, Q]) provides the baseline p(l|v) via causal masking, yet the posterior branch is the one used for control at inference. The role of the stop-gradient and why degrading the baseline is avoided is asserted rather than demonstrated, and a shared-weight self-cancellation effect (updating the numerator also shifts the stop-grad denominator) is not discussed.

Numerical inconsistencies reduce confidence: the abstract states an 11.3% OOD improvement while contribution 3 in the introduction states 8.8%; the ablation text says 'full LangForce (63.5%)' while Table 5 reports 66.5%.

Reproducibility red flags: the code link is a placeholder ('available at this'), and the reference list contains future-dated arXiv identifiers (e.g., arXiv:2604.05014, 2603.24393, 2601.14133, 2601.02456) and mismatched years (Bjorck et al., 2026 vs 2025a/2025b), making several key references (including the StarVLA framework the method is built on) unverifiable.

Evidence for the shortcut is largely indirect. The main pilot experiments train a separate vision-only model rather than testing whether the full language-conditioned model ignores language at inference (e.g., via counterfactual or corrupted instructions). The Appendix NLL/PPL proxy (Table 7) is suggestive but not a direct causal test.

Evaluation lacks error bars or significance tests, and some margins are small (RoboCasa 52.6 vs 48.8; real-world 1-block 25/30 ties pi0.5 25/30). The SOTA claim rests on a single backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B) and baseline numbers are drawn from heterogeneous sources with different training data, which weakens the fairness of the comparison.

The real-world and LIBERO gains are modest and the authors themselves note the tasks primarily test instruction following rather than dexterous manipulation; this limits the reach of the claimed improvements.

strengths: The paper identifies and motivates a genuinely interesting and practically important failure mode ('vision shortcut' / information collapse) in VLA training, and supports it with three systematic pilot experiments (RoboCasa, LIBERO Goal, BridgeDataV2+Fractal) that show vision-only models nearly match language-conditioned baselines on ID data but collapse on ambiguous (LIBERO Goal 9.8%) and OOD (SimplerEnv ~0%) settings.

Broad and consistent empirical validation: state-of-the-art results on SimplerEnv (66.5% vs 55.2% for the same-framework baseline), RoboCasa (52.6%), LIBERO (98.4%, with the largest gain on the ambiguous Goal suite), plus two real-world Franka pick-and-place tasks, and an honest attempt to separate instruction-following from low-level control.

The Latent Action Queries design is a clean, practical architectural contribution: it acts as a bottleneck and, importantly, inference uses only the posterior branch, so there is no test-time overhead. The O(K^2) vs O(N^2) conditioning argument is a nice efficiency point.

The observation that LangForce preserves text-only conversational ability while the QwenGR00T baseline degenerates into gibberish is a useful and somewhat surprising side-benefit, and the auxiliary p(l|v) control (Table 10) makes a reasonable effort to disentangle language retention from action-relevant grounding.
The limitations discussion is honest (training overhead, simple real-world tasks) and the ablations over lambda, beta, and number of queries provide reasonable sensitivity analysis.
weaknesses: The implemented objective (Eq. 7) is difficult to reconcile with the stated theory (Eq. 4). In the prior branch the queries Q appear before l and attend only to v, so H_Q^prior is a deterministic function of v; information-theoretically it cannot add information about l beyond v, so maximizing log p(l | v, H_Q^prior) (with a stop-grad denominator) appears to encourage overfitting the training scene-to-instruction mapping — the very shortcut the paper claims to penalize. The derivation connecting the language-log-prob proxy to the action-level LLR, the exact computation of the stop-gradient baseline log p(l | v), and the gradient flow through H_Q^prior (given that H_Q^prior is detached for L_prior) are all underspecified. This is the central mechanism and it needs to be made precise and justified.

Numerical inconsistencies: the abstract states an 11.3% OOD improvement while the introduction states 8.8%; the ablation text says 'the full LangForce (63.5%)' and reports a +6.0% boost, whereas Table 5 lists LangForce at 66.5% (66.5 - 57.5 = 9.0). Table 11 is captioned as a beta ablation but reports lambda. These errors undermine confidence in the results.

Baseline fairness: many baselines are copied from their original papers with different training data and protocols, and the paper only asserts that 'the training datasets for these baselines encompass the data used in our experiments.' Only QwenGR00T is trained within the same StarVLA framework, so the headline cross-paper comparisons (e.g., vs pi-0.5, Isaac-GR00T) are not apples-to-apples.

No confidence intervals or significance tests are reported despite large trial counts (480 on SimplerEnv, 50/task on RoboCasa). Some per-task gains are small (SimplerEnv 'Stack Green Block' 29.2 -> 33.3), and the RoboCasa average gain over the baseline is modest (+4.8).

Limited novelty relative to prior work: the paper itself notes BayesVLA (Xu et al., 2025) already performs Bayesian decomposition of VLA policies, and the main claimed distinction is single-stage vs two-stage training plus the latent queries. The contribution is therefore incremental.

The claim of preserving general multimodal capabilities is supported only qualitatively (a single math example in Figures 4-6) with no quantitative evaluation, while the appendix concedes that general vision-language (image+text) ability still degrades.

Reproducibility concerns: the code/video URL appears to be a placeholder ('available at this'), and key implementation details (how the log p(l | v) baseline is obtained, exact loss weighting schedule) are not specified well enough to reproduce.
